PROBATE HOMESTEAD SET-ASIDE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

PURPOSE OF THIS PROBATE HOMESTEAD INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California's probate homestead set-aside, codified at Probate Code §§ 6520-6528 (Division 6, Part 3, Chapter 3, "Setting Aside Probate Homestead"). It concerns a probate court's discretionary power, exercised during the court-supervised administration of a decedent's estate, to select and set apart a homestead for the use of a surviving spouse and/or minor children. This is a distinct statutory mechanism from an automatic homestead exemption or a recorded declared homestead that protects a living person's equity from creditors during that person's lifetime; the probate homestead set-aside described here can arise only after a person's death and only through a probate court proceeding, under the Probate Code rather than the Code of Civil Procedure. This Information Sheet concerns the estate of Pat Morgan, who died on March 15, 2026, with respect to property that may include the property located at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, and is prepared in connection with a potential petition by Jordan Lee. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing California statutes; it is not a court filing, a petition, an order, or legal advice about whether a probate homestead will be set aside, what property or terms a court would select, or any other outcome specific to Pat Morgan's estate or Jordan Lee's circumstances.

WHO MAY PETITION, AND FOR WHOSE USE A PROBATE HOMESTEAD MAY BE SET APART
Probate Code § 6520 gives a probate court discretion, upon the filing of the inventory or at any later time during administration of the estate, to select and set apart one probate homestead on petition, in the manner the chapter provides. Probate Code § 6521 states that the probate homestead is set apart for the use of one or more of two categories of persons: (a) the surviving spouse, and (b) the minor children of the decedent. Probate Code § 6525(a) states who may file the petition that starts this process: "any interested person," not only the surviving spouse or a minor child (or someone acting for a minor child).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Upon the filing of the inventory or at any subsequent time during the administration of the estate, the court in its discretion may on petition therefor select and set apart one probate homestead in the manner provided in this chapter."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6520, California Probate Code, existence and timing of the court's discretionary power to set apart a probate homestead (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6520.)
  "The probate homestead shall be set apart for the use of one or more of the following persons: (a) The surviving spouse. (b) The minor children of the decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6521, California Probate Code, persons for whose use a probate homestead is set apart (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6521.)
  "A petition to select and set apart a probate homestead may be filed by any interested person."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6525(a), California Probate Code, who may file a petition to select and set apart a probate homestead (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6525.)
  Known gap: Probate Code §§ 6520, 6521, and 6525 are separately numbered, independently enacted sections of the same chapter, so they are independent sources of one another. This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of § 6525; subdivision (a) also cross-references notice requirements under Probate Code § 1220, and § 6525(b) separately lists three categories of persons entitled to notice of the hearing — those notice provisions were fetched as part of the same primary-source text but are not restated or quoted in this clause. This clause states who the statute allows to petition and for whose use the homestead may be set apart; it does not state whether a probate court would grant a set-aside on the facts of any particular case, which is a matter left to the court's discretion under other sections of this chapter.

PROPERTY ELIGIBLE TO BE SELECTED AS A PROBATE HOMESTEAD
Probate Code § 6522(a) sets an order of preference for what property a probate homestead may be selected from, giving first preference to community and quasi-community property, or property owned in common by the decedent and the person entitled to have the homestead set apart. If the homestead is for the surviving spouse, or the surviving spouse and minor children, it is drawn from community or quasi-community property; if for the surviving spouse, or minor children, or both, it may also be drawn from property owned in common by the decedent and the persons entitled to the homestead, from the decedent's separate property, or, if the decedent was unmarried at death, from property the decedent owned. Section 6522(b) limits this further: the probate homestead cannot be selected out of property in which the right to possession is vested in a third person unless that third person consents, where a "third person" is someone whose right to possession existed at, or arose upon, the decedent's death and was not created by testate or intestate succession from the decedent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The probate homestead shall be selected out of the following property, giving first preference to the community and quasi-community property of, or property owned in common by, the decedent and the person entitled to have the homestead set apart: (1) If the homestead is set apart for the use of the surviving spouse or for the use of the surviving spouse and minor children, out of community property or quasi-community property. (2) If the homestead is set apart for the use of the surviving spouse or for the use of the minor children or for the use of the surviving spouse and minor children, out of property owned in common by the decedent and the persons entitled to have the homestead set apart, or out of the separate property of the decedent or, if the decedent was not married at the time of death, out of property owned by the decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6522(a), California Probate Code, order of preference for property from which a probate homestead may be selected (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6522.)
  "The probate homestead shall not be selected out of property the right to possession of which is vested in a third person unless the third person consents thereto. As used in this subdivision, “third person” means a person whose right to possession of the property (1) existed at the time of the death of the decedent or came into existence upon the death of the decedent and (2) was not created by testate or intestate succession from the decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6522(b), California Probate Code, limit on selecting property in which a third person's right of possession is vested (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6522.)
  Known gap: Probate Code §§ 6522(a) and 6522(b) are both subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another as sources. This clause states the property-selection rules on their face; it does not determine what property is community property, quasi-community property, separate property, or property owned in common as to any specific decedent's estate, and it does not determine whether any specific person qualifies as a "third person" under § 6522(b).

THE COURT'S DISCRETION: FACTORS CONSIDERED AND TERMS OF THE SET-ASIDE
Probate Code § 6523(a) lists the factors a court must consider in selecting and setting apart a probate homestead: the needs of the surviving spouse and minor children; liens and encumbrances on the property; the claims of creditors; the needs of the decedent's heirs or devisees; and the decedent's intent regarding the property and the decedent's estate plan, as shown by inter vivos and testamentary transfers or other means. Section 6523(b) then directs the court, in light of those factors and other relevant considerations within its discretion, to (1) select the most appropriate available property suitable for use as a homestead, including adjoining property beyond the dwelling itself where reasonable, and (2) set the homestead apart for a term and upon conditions the court considers proper, which may include conditions such as the homestead recipient assigning other property to the decedent's heirs or devisees. The statutory text does not itself state a fixed dollar value limit or a fixed duration for a probate homestead; instead, it commits both the term and the conditions of the set-aside to the court's discretion, applied to the factors listed in subdivision (a).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In selecting and setting apart the probate homestead, the court shall consider the needs of the surviving spouse and minor children, the liens and encumbrances on the property, the claims of creditors, the needs of the heirs or devisees of the decedent, and the intent of the decedent with respect to the property in the estate and the estate plan of the decedent as expressed in inter vivos and testamentary transfers or by other means."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6523(a), California Probate Code, factors the court must consider in selecting and setting apart a probate homestead (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6523.)
  "The court, in light of subdivision (a) and other relevant considerations as determined by the court in its discretion, shall: (1) Select as a probate homestead the most appropriate property available that is suitable for that use, including in addition to the dwelling itself such adjoining property as appears reasonable. (2) Set the probate homestead so selected apart for such a term and upon such conditions (including, but not limited to, assignment by the homestead recipient of other property to the heirs or devisees of the property set apart as a homestead) as appear proper."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6523(b), California Probate Code, the court's discretion to select property and set the term and conditions of the homestead (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6523.)
  Known gap: Probate Code §§ 6523(a) and 6523(b) are both subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another as sources. This clause states that the fetched statutory text does not itself impose a fixed dollar-value cap or a fixed term of years; it does not independently verify the absence of any such limit elsewhere in the Probate Code or in case law construing this chapter, and it does not describe how a court would weigh the listed factors against one another in any specific case.

DURATION OF THE SET-ASIDE AND ITS EFFECT ON ESTATE ADMINISTRATION
Probate Code § 6524 caps how long a probate homestead may last: it may be set apart only for a limited period designated in the court's order, and in no case beyond the surviving spouse's lifetime or, as to a child, beyond that child's minority. The same section states that the decedent's property remains subject to administration, including testate and intestate succession, subject to the probate homestead right — meaning the set-aside does not remove the property from the estate or from the succession process, but instead creates a right that the ongoing administration and succession are subject to for the designated period. Section 6524 further provides that, to the extent applicable, the parties' rights during the period the probate homestead is set apart are governed by the Legal Estates Principal and Income Law, Chapter 2.6 (commencing with Section 731) of Title 2 of Part 1 of Division 2 of the Civil Code.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The property set apart as a probate homestead shall be set apart only for a limited period, to be designated in the order, and in no case beyond the lifetime of the surviving spouse, or, as to a child, beyond its minority. Subject to the probate homestead right, the property of the decedent remains subject to administration including testate and intestate succession. The rights of the parties during the period for which the probate homestead is set apart are governed, to the extent applicable, by the Legal Estates Principal and Income Law, Chapter 2.6 (commencing with Section 731) of Title 2 of Part 1 of Division 2 of the Civil Code."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6524, California Probate Code, outer time limits on a probate homestead and its relationship to ongoing estate administration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6524.)
  Known gap: This clause relies on a single statutory section, Probate Code § 6524; no second, independent source is cited for these specific duration and administration-effect rules. Section 6524 cross-references the Legal Estates Principal and Income Law (Civil Code §§ 731 et seq.) for the parties' rights during the set-aside period; that cross-referenced law was not independently fetched or verified for this clause, so this clause does not describe what those provisions say. This clause also does not describe the separate circumstances under which a court may modify or terminate a probate homestead right before the outer limits stated here are reached, which this Information Sheet does not address.

PRIORITY OF THE PROBATE HOMESTEAD RIGHT RELATIVE TO CREDITORS' CLAIMS
Probate Code § 6526 states three rules about how the probate homestead right relates to claims against the estate. Under § 6526(a), property set apart as a probate homestead remains liable for claims against the decedent's estate, subject to the probate homestead right itself; the probate homestead right in that property is liable for claims secured by liens and encumbrances that existed on the property at the time of the decedent's death, but is exempt, to the extent of the homestead exemption, from any claim that would have been subject to a homestead exemption at the time of death under Code of Civil Procedure Article 4 (commencing with § 704.710) of Chapter 4, Division 2, Title 9, Part 2. Under § 6526(b), the probate homestead right is not liable for claims against the person for whose use the homestead is set apart. Under § 6526(c), property set apart as a probate homestead remains liable, after administration, for claims against the decedent's testate or intestate successors or other successors to the property, again subject to the probate homestead right.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Property of the decedent set apart as a probate homestead is liable for claims against the estate of the decedent, subject to the probate homestead right. The probate homestead right in property of the decedent is liable for claims that are secured by liens and encumbrances on the property at the time of the decedent’s death but is exempt to the extent of the homestead exemption as to any claim that would have been subject to a homestead exemption at the time of the decedent’s death under Article 4 (commencing with Section 704.710) of Chapter 4 of Division 2 of Title 9 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6526(a), California Probate Code, liability of a probate homestead for lien-secured claims and its exemption to the extent of the homestead exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6526.)
  "The probate homestead right in the property of the decedent is not liable for claims against the person for whose use the probate homestead is set apart."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6526(b), California Probate Code, non-liability of the probate homestead right for claims against the homestead recipient personally (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6526.)
  "Property of the decedent set apart as a probate homestead is liable for claims against the testate or intestate successors of the decedent or other successors to the property after administration, subject to the probate homestead right."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6526(c), California Probate Code, continued liability of the property for claims against successors after administration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6526.)
  Known gap: Probate Code §§ 6526(a), 6526(b), and 6526(c) are all subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another as sources. Section 6526(a) cross-references the Code of Civil Procedure's homestead-exemption Article 4 (commencing with § 704.710) to define the scope of its own exemption from lien-secured claims; this clause does not restate or re-verify the current dollar-amount formula under that cross-referenced Code of Civil Procedure article, which is addressed in this corpus's separate homestead exemption information sheet and was not re-fetched for this clause. This clause states the statutory liability and exemption rules as written; it does not determine how those rules would apply to any specific claim, lien, or encumbrance against a specific decedent's estate.

THIS CHAPTER DOES NOT AFFECT A SEPARATE DECLARATION OF HOMESTEAD
Probate Code § 6528 expressly states that nothing in this chapter terminates or otherwise affects a declaration of homestead by, or for the benefit of, a surviving spouse or minor child of the decedent with respect to the community, quasi-community, or common interest of the surviving spouse or minor child in property in the decedent's estate; the statute adds that this section is declaratory of, and does not constitute a change in, existing law. On its face, this confirms that the probate homestead set-aside described in this Information Sheet is a distinct right from a declaration of homestead, and that a probate court's action (or inaction) under this chapter does not by itself terminate or otherwise affect any such separate declaration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Nothing in this chapter terminates or otherwise affects a declaration of homestead by, or for the benefit of, a surviving spouse or minor child of the decedent with respect to the community, quasi-community, or common interest of the surviving spouse or minor child in property in the decedent’s estate. This section is declaratory of, and does not constitute a change in, existing law."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6528, California Probate Code, this chapter does not terminate or affect a separate declaration of homestead (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6528.)
  Known gap: This clause relies on a single statutory section, Probate Code § 6528; no second, independent source is cited for this specific point. Section 6528 refers to "a declaration of homestead" without itself defining that term or citing the Code of Civil Procedure provisions that create declared homesteads or the automatic homestead exemption; this clause does not describe what protections a declaration of homestead provides, which is addressed in this corpus's separate homestead exemption information sheet (covering Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.710-704.995) and was not re-verified here.
